extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural designers, students of architecture, and critics interested in principles of beauty and ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines for creating and judging architectural beauty and ornamentation, emphasizing natural imitation, massing, placement, and the avoidance of unnatural decorative forms. Covers what constitutes ornament, where it should be placed, how it should be treated architecturally, and examples of good and bad practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of mass and breadth for majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative majesty of buildings depends more on the weight and vigor of their masses than on any other attribute of their design: mass of everything, of bulk, of light, of darkness, of color — breadth of them; not broken light, nor scattered darkness, nor divided weight, but solid stone, broad sunshine, starless shade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should aim for broad, simple, and solid masses to convey power. Small, divided, or excessively detailed elements reduce majesty. Examples of effective means: penthouse roofs over belfry lights, sloping roofs, jutting porches, projecting balconies, hollow niches, massy gargoyles, frowning parapets. Even clumsy means are acceptable if they secure gloom (deep shadow) and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor broad dark simple forms over fine subdivision
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad, dark, and simple forms produce delight and strength; multiplicity of fine lines (e.g., thin cross-bars) is uninteresting and contradicts architectural lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiplying small sharp details (like Venetian-blind-style cross-bars in belfries). Prefer a few grand masses of shadow and simple sweeping curves which may be more delightful than fine stone-work because of their breadth and tone (moss, lichen, grey slopes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament should be imitative of common natural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: All beautiful lines are adaptations of those which are commonest in the external creation; in proportion to the richness of their association, the resemblance to natural work must be more closely attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forms drawn from plants, animals, human figure, rocks, water, clouds, etc. The highest ornament imitates higher orders of existence (human form most noble). Imitation is not slavish copying but adoption of natural types and associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-resonance test (frequency-to-beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms not taken from natural objects are likely to be ugly; forms most frequent in the visible world may be assumed most beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proposed ornament by whether similar forms are habitually encountered in nature; prefer those shapes which are visibly frequent and associated with beauty. This is an operational test to distinguish natural-feeling ornament from monstrous/unfamiliar designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curves are the primary source of beauty; straight lines only when natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Most perfectly beautiful forms must be composed of curves since straight lines are rare in nature; when straight lines are necessary they should be arranged consistent with natural groupings of straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept straight-lined ornament only if it echoes common crystalline or naturally occurring angular forms; otherwise favor curved, organic lines. Example: Lombard ornaments (Pisa) can be justified by natural crystalline analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornaments lacking natural precedent (Greek fret / guilloche)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments which have no natural precedent, such as the Greek fret (guilloche), are monstrous and ugly because they resemble forms (e.g., bismuth crystals) that are rare and not part of everyday visual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain fillets or plinths to such harsh concatenations of straight lines except where used as foil to true ornament or on extremely small scale (coins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg-and-dart moulding as example of successful imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The egg-and-dart moulding is beautiful because it imitates familiar natural forms (pebbles and the flattened oval), and subtle details (flattened upper surface) are essential to its perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the precise natural detail (e.g., the flattening of the 'egg'); omission of such subtleties makes the ornament vulgar. Use natural observation to refine ornament shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-lined Lombard ornament permitted by crystalline precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Lombard ornament composed of right lines can be defended because its outline corresponds to common crystalline forms (e.g., salt crystals, oxides, sulphurets), making it a graceful and appropriate combination of straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification for geometric or angular ornament should be explicit: show its relation to frequent natural crystalline structures to avoid the charge of unnaturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject small-scale reticulation/portcullis on solid surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Tudor reticulation (portcullis-like netting), when diminished and set on a solid surface, is ugly; it lacks the natural variation of reticulation and loses dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reticulated texture is desired, reveal shade through bars and keep scale and variation. Avoid tiny, repetitive mesh carved flat on a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heraldic decoration should be sparing and read as inscription, not ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Heraldic devices have pride and significance appropriate in certain places (over gates, in painted windows, bosses), but as repeated surface decoration they are commonly ugly and destroy a building's power and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full coats/arms in a few prominent locations; for frequent repetition choose a single fair, simple symbol (e.g., fleur-de-lis, Florentine giglio, English rose) rather than a King's arms. Treat heraldry as inscription rather than surface ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscriptions/letters are non-natural and should be used only for legible purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are among the most unnatural forms and should only be endured where their intellectual meaning is more important than ornament; they are offences to the eye when mere decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place inscriptions where they will be read. Make writing plain and legible; do not ornament or distort letters (no tails/dashes that hinder reading). Use architectural silence around inscriptions so they serve their function without distracting from composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flying scrolls and ribands as ornamental forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribands and flying scrolls are unlike natural, structured forms (seaweed, grass) which have skeletons and graded substance; ribands have no structure and therefore cannot fall or wave gracefullly — they are vile as ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce ribands as ornament. If inscription is necessary, prefer a tablet or plain roll understood as a support for text rather than an ornamental flying scroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery is only noble when it expresses motion or gravitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery is ignoble as an independent subject; it is valuable only when it exponentiates motion (flowing) or gravitation (sweeping mass revealing weight), serving to express other higher things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drapery to show motion (e.g., blown garments) or to indicate weight and repose (sweeping veils that conceal feet). Avoid drapery used for its own sake or as delicate purely decorative fabric without structural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place plant/flower ornament where nature would place it; avoid unnatural garlands/festoons
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetable ornament must be placed and associated as nature would place it; unnatural arrangements (e.g., heavy bunches pinned on walls, garlands hung on walls) destroy value and are ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce pendent tendrils or boughs only where appropriate (luxuriant decoration) and place flowerwork into capitals or positions where natural growth would occur. Do not hang garlands on flat walls; use medallions, solid rings, or colored marble circles if a circular motif is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petty excrescences that break noble terminal forms (dripstone 'handle')
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, unrelated decorative projections (e.g., dripstones shaped like chest-of-drawers handles over square-headed windows) are offensive because they break the unity and power of the square form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a square head as exponent of power, keep its space unbroken and mouldings severe, or associate the square with circular traceries. Do not cut or turn out its lines with isolated, glued-on ornaments that have no harmony with structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural ornament must show connected/rooted structure (treatment renders something architectural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative forms are architectural when treated so that they suggest natural roots and connections (e.g., Corinthian capital expands under the abacus as Nature would; flamboyant leaf mouldings nestle and clasp shafts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give ornament indications of connected structure and order (counting, placing, and fitting into hollows and angles) so they appear natural and architectural rather than pasted-on. Ornament must look as if it 'belongs' and grows from the part it decorates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold enquiry for ornament: place, treatment, and color
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine right ornament, consider (1) the right place for architectural ornament, (2) the peculiar treatment that renders ornament architectural, and (3) the right use of color associated with imitative form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three heads as a framework when designing or judging ornament: ensure ornament is located where nature suggests, treated so as to be structurally and visually integrated, and colored in ways that support its imitative and architectural role (note: full guidance on color follows elsewhere).
